Collection of my Defender 'Research Material' in an attempt to understand the games 'AI' and mechanics. 

Q: How  many enemies spawn per level? What are the rules that govern their spawning? :
-----------

There are strict limits on how many primary enemies spawn at the start of each level (wave) in the original arcade version of [Defender](https://www.google.com/search?q=defender&kgmid=/m/02k4l6#sv=CBwSqwQK-). However, there is no limit to how many Baiters can appear if you take too long to clear a stage. 
The exact enemy limits and spawn behaviors break down as follows:
## Fixed Spawn Limits per Wave
The game caps the maximum number of primary targets that exist at the start of a level. According to the [Arcade Database](https://adb.arcadeitalia.net/dettaglio_mame.php?game_name=defender), the standard wave compositions are: 

* **Wave 1**: 15 Landers (No Bombers or Pods).
* **Wave 2**: 20 Landers, 3 Bombers, and 1 Pod.
* **Wave 3**: 20 Landers, 4 Bombers, and 3 Pods.
* **Waves 4 and Up**: 20 Landers, 5 Bombers, and 4 Pods. 

## Reactive and Unlimited Spawns
While the starting numbers are hard-capped, other enemies are triggered dynamically by game events:

* **Mutants**: There is a strict limit of 10 Mutants that can spawn naturally from abductions per wave because there are only 10 humanoids on the map. (Note: If the planet explodes because all humanoids die, the level instantly fills entirely with Mutants.) 
* **Swarmers**: They do not have a set wave limit; instead, exactly 4 to 5 Swarmers are locked inside each Pod. Destroying a Pod releases them instantly.
* **Baiters**: These serve as the game's anti-stalling mechanic. They `“appear out of thin air when you are not fast enough” and “there is no limit in the amount of them appearing.”, according to [Unity Community Discussion](https://discussions.unity.com/t/enemy-behaviour-of-the-williams-defender-classic-arcade-machine/730917). If you linger on a level, the game will continually spawn them to hunt you down.

## How Enemy Spawning and Pacing Works
The original [Defender](https://www.google.com/search?q=defender&kgmid=/m/02k4l6#sv=CBwSqwQK-) does not drop all of its capped enemies onto the screen simultaneously. Instead, it uses a precise, hardcoded progression system designed to keep the player constantly moving across the wraparound planet map. 

* **The Initial Drop**: When a wave begins, the game distributes a baseline layout of Pods, Bombers, and a few Landers across the long, scrolling terrain.
* **The Scanning Group Logic**: Landers do not spawn individually; they enter the map in small "scanning groups" or squads. As you hunt down and destroy the active Landers, the game triggers the next waiting squad to warp in.
* **Off-Screen Activity**: Crucially, enemies spawn and act even when they are not on your immediate screen. The long-range "Radar" (scanner) at the top of the monitor is mandatory for high-level play because it lets you track Landers capturing humanoids miles away from your position.
* **The Baiter Pacing Clock**: The master pacing mechanic is completely time-based. The game tracks how long a wave is taking. If you play too defensively or fail to clear enemies fast enough, the game forces the aggressive Baiters to spawn, shifting the pacing from a strategic rescue mission into frantic survival. 

------------------------------
## The Famous Wave 256 "Glitch"
In early 1980s arcade hardware, memory was incredibly scarce. To track the current level, Defender's legendary developer, Eugene Jarvis, allocated a single 8-bit byte of memory for the level counter.


* **The 8-Bit Overflow**: An 8-bit integer can only count from 0 to 255. When an expert player successfully beats Wave 255, the counter automatically resets and "wraps around" to Wave 0.
* **The Resetting Difficulty Counter**: The hardware handles this roll-over much more gracefully than Pac-Man's famous game-ending split-screen glitch. Instead of crashing, corrupting the graphics, or trapping you in an un-winnable screen, the code simply reads Wave 0 as Wave 1 difficulty.
* **The Reward**: After surviving 255 grueling levels of pure chaos, the game suddenly treats the player to a slow, incredibly easy wave identical to the very first level of the game. For elite arcade players, reaching Wave 256 is the ultimate milestone because it rewards them with a massive breather to easily build back up their ships and smart bombs.

## The Brutal "Space Level" (Null Space) Mechanic
If you fail your core mission and let the aliens abduct all 10 humanoids, the planet's surface violently explodes. You are thrust into a pitch-black void known as Null Space, triggering a dramatic and terrifying shift in gameplay:

* **Instant Mutation**: The moment the terrain is destroyed, every single Lander remaining on the map instantly transforms into a hyper-aggressive Mutant. 
* **The Mutant Swarm**: Because Mutants are the fastest enemies and fly directly at your ship in relentless zig-zag patterns, surviving a Space Level is considered a true badge of honor among elite arcade players.
* **Planet Restoration**: To escape Null Space, you must completely clear the current wave of its hyper-fast enemies. The game forces you to survive this hellscape across successive rounds until Wave 5 (or every 5th wave thereafter), at which point the humanoids are replenished and the mountainous planet surface safely reforms. 
* **The "Carry" Strategy**: Pro players discovered a clever loophole to bypass the destruction. If you are down to your last human and know you cannot protect him, you can deliberately shoot or catch him and hold him in your ship's cargo without depositing him back on the surface. As long as you finish the level while physically holding that single human, the planet will not explode, allowing you to bypass Null Space entirely for the next wave. 


------------------------------
## The Notoriously Complex Arcade Control Panel
Defender is widely remembered for having one of the most unorthodox and physically demanding control layouts in arcade history. Instead of a standard joystick that moves in all four directions, developer Eugene Jarvis split the ship's movement and speed across an asymmetric layout of a two-way vertical joystick and five separate buttons.
The panel forces players to use both hands to orchestrate simultaneous actions across the deck:

* **Left Hand (The Joystick)**: Controls a heavy-duty, two-way optical joystick that only moves up and down. You use this hand strictly to adjust your altitude on the screen.
* **Right Hand (The Combat Array)**: Your right hand hovers over a cluster of arcade buttons to manage the ship's velocity and firepower:
* **Reverse Button**: Flips the orientation of your ship left or right. Because the joystick doesn't steer, you must tap this constantly to turn around.
   * **Thrust Button**: Acts like a car's gas pedal. You hold it down to accelerate forward in whichever direction your ship is facing.
   * **Fire Button**: Rapidly fires your horizontal laser weapon.
* **Emergency Buttons (Center/Thumb)**:
* **Smart Bomb**: Detonates a screen-clearing blast that obliterates all nearby enemies. These are rare and must be conserved for dangerous Pod clusters.
   * **Hyperspace**: A panic button positioned far away from the main cluster. Pressing it warps you to a random spot on the map, but carries a high risk of materializing directly into an enemy or exploding instantly.

This setup created an intense learning curve, requiring players to master the rhythm of holding Thrust, tapping Fire, and slamming Reverse to weave through incoming alien fire. 

Q: Are there specific rules to where humans appear on the serface?
--------

There is no set geographical pattern to where the [humans](https://www.google.com/search?q=humans&kgmid=/g/11trgvp76m#) (humanoids) appear across the landscape; their initial placement at the start of a wave is entirely randomized by the game's code. 
However, they do follow strict behavioral and hardware rules regarding how and where they exist on the map:

### 1. Grounded Constraints
Humanoids are strictly bound to the terrain. They are randomly distributed across the long, wraparound map, but they will only spawn directly on top of the jagged mountain line. They cannot float or wander into the sky on their own. While they can walk around slowly on the ground, they will never voluntarily leave the mountain surface. 
### 2. The Spacing Conflict Bug
Because humanoids are placed randomly by the software, the game occasionally tries to spawn two or more humans on the exact same coordinate. The game's engine cannot handle overlapping humanoids. When this happens, a spacing conflict occurs, forcing the overlapping humans to forcefully scatter. 
If the terrain at that coordinate is exceptionally low, this glitch can actually launch a humanoid high into the sky. They will then slowly drift straight down back to the planet's surface like a skydiver. 
### 3. Complete Population Resets
The total human population acts as a fixed counter.


* **The Starting Number**: Every fresh game begins with exactly 10 humanoids scattered across the map. 
* **Persistence Between Waves**: If you finish Wave 1 with only 4 humans surviving, Wave 2 will start with those exact same 4 humans left in their last known positions. The game does not automatically replenish your population between rounds.
* **The 5-Wave Rule**: The only time the population pattern fully resets is at the start of every 5th wave (Waves 5, 10, 15, etc.). At this milestone, the planet's population is completely restored back to 10 brand-new, randomly scattered humans. 

### 4. Player-Driven Patterns
While the game starts with random placement, high-level players completely disrupt this by physically moving the humans. When you rescue a falling human, you can fly down to the ground to drop him off. Expert players will deliberately gather multiple humans and drop them off in one specific "safe zone" on the map, creating a concentrated cluster that is much easier to guard against incoming Landers.

## How exactly do the enemies 'move'?

The exact flight and targeting mechanics for each enemy type are outlined below to help you implement them in code.

------------------------------

### 1. Landers: The Scanning Routine
[Landers](https://www.google.com/search?q=landers&kgmid=/g/11k547ht2l#sv=CBwSrgQK-) have two states: searching and abducting.

* The Search State (Horizontal Vectoring): [Landers](https://www.google.com/search?q=landers&kgmid=/g/11k547ht2l#sv=CBwSrgQK-) randomly drift horizontally across the wrapping world map, roughly patrolling the lower half of the screen near the mountains.
* **The "Lock-On" Check**: A Lander does not constantly track a human. Instead, it periodically checks the world coordinates. When a Lander flies within a certain horizontal radius of a humanoid on the ground, its state changes to Abduct.
* **The Abduction Lift**: Once locked on, the Lander drops vertically straight down at a fixed speed, latches onto the human, and begins flying vertically straight up toward the top edge of the screen. 
* **The Shooting Logic**: [Landers](https://www.google.com/search?q=landers&kgmid=/g/11k547ht2l#sv=CBwSrgQK-) do not shoot at the player accurately. They have an internal timer (e.g., every 1–2 seconds) that fires a projectile in the general direction of the player's coordinate, adding a large random offset to ensure the shot is sloppy. 

### 2. [Mutants](https://www.google.com/search?q=mutants&kgmid=/g/11trgvpwkw#sv=CBwSrgQK-): Absolute Intercept
[Mutants](https://www.google.com/search?q=mutants&kgmid=/g/11trgvpwkw#sv=CBwSrgQK-) are hyper-aggressive and act as absolute homing missiles directed at the player.

* **Targeting Vec2**: Every frame, a Mutant calculates a normalized vector directly from its current position (x1, y1) to your ship’s position (x2, y2).
* **The Zig-Zag Offset**: If they flew perfectly straight, they would be too easy to shoot. The original game adds a rapid, alternating sine-wave or zig-zag pattern perpendicular to their main travel vector.
* **Implementation tip**: Calculate the base velocity vector toward the player, then alternate adding a minor horizontal or vertical offset using an internal game timer to achieve that "erratic jitter". 

### 3. Bombers: Static Screen Patrolling
Bombers are completely oblivious to the player and serve as passive screen-hazards. [6, 10] 

* **Horizontal-Only Domai**n: Bombers choose a fixed altitude (usually higher up in the atmosphere) and drift strictly horizontally. They occasionally reverse direction if they bounce off the boundaries of the screen width.
* **Mine Dropping**: They have a strict drop timer. As they drift, they spawn stationary particle mines behind them. To code this accurately, the mines should have a speed of zero—they should hang in space exactly where they were spawned, forcing the player to fly around them. 

### 4. Swarmers: Group Cohesion and Lagged Chasing
[Swarmers](https://www.google.com/search?q=swarmers&kgmid=/g/11sf80jxr3#sv=CBwSrwQK-) are small, incredibly fast, and are designed to overwhelm you. 

* **The Cohesion Vector**: Swarmers do not track you individually. They use a "group logic" where all Swarmers spawned from a single Pod share a direction.
* **Lagged Overtaking**: [Swarmers](https://www.google.com/search?q=swarmers&kgmid=/g/11sf80jxr3#sv=CBwSrwQK-) fly in a straight path toward the player's last known location. They move so quickly that they frequently overshoot you.
* **The Turn-Around Rule**: Crucially, [Swarmers](https://www.google.com/search?q=swarmers&kgmid=/g/11sf80jxr3#sv=CBwSrwQK-) cannot turn around instantly. If you tap "Reverse" and fly past them, the [Swarmers](https://www.google.com/search?q=swarmers&kgmid=/g/11sf80jxr3#sv=CBwSrwQK-) are forced to continue flying in their original direction for a split second before their path-adjustment algorithm allowed them to swing around and chase you again. 

### 5. [Baiters](https://www.google.com/search?q=baiters&kgmid=/g/11gmg7gbv2#sv=CBwSrgQK-): Relative Velocity and Position Sampling (The Most Crucial Code)
[Baiters](https://www.google.com/search?q=baiters&kgmid=/g/11gmg7gbv2#sv=CBwSrgQK--Dg) are famously difficult because of a highly specific algorithmic trick. They do not track you in real-time. Instead, they use a Periodic Sampling Clock.
, according to [Doug's World](https://www.dougmahugh.com/defender-chapter07/).

* **The Memory Trap**: If a [Baiter](https://www.google.com/search?q=baiter&kgmid=/g/11gmg7gbv2#-gK) checks your position and you are at (100, 200), it locks that coordinate in its memory and flies straight there. If you stay at a constant speed, it easily intercepts you. If you suddenly slam on the brakes, change altitude, or hit "Reverse", the Baiter will fly directly to where you used to be, overshooting you completely.
* **Relative Speed Buff**: [Baiters](https://www.google.com/search?q=baiters&kgmid=/g/11gmg7gbv2#sv=CBwSrgQK-) are programmed to be faster than you. Jarvis coded this by taking the player's current velocity vector and adding it to the Baiter's base velocity.
* **The Pro-Tip Glitch**: “A [baiter](https://www.google.com/search?q=baiter&kgmid=/g/11gmg7gbv2#-8bgJ) that is very close to you will never try to run into you if you don't move.”, as noted by Doug's World. If you sit completely still, the [Baiter](https://www.google.com/search?q=baiter&kgmid=/g/11gmg7gbv2#)'s relative velocity calculation drops significantly, causing it to hover right next to you rather than ramming you (though it will still shoot you). 

## Summary

To get it right, you have to match its highly unorthodox 1980s AI mechanics. Because the original arcade processor was highly restricted, developer Eugene Jarvis didn't use advanced pathfinding; instead, he used sampling clocks, absolute map vectors, and relative velocity tracking.
